punch: And the experiment that proved it is 20 years old.

headline: Everyone treats fusion
body: Stay open longer, beat the clock, grow taller. That's the model almost every height protocol is built on.
punch: It has the causality backwards — and once you see why a lot of advice stops making sense.

headline: The experiment
body: Researchers transplanted growth plates between animals of different ages. If the body controlled growth rate, a transplanted plate would grow at the recipient's pace. It didn't. A young plate in an old animal grew fast. An old plate in a young animal stayed slow.
punch: Growth rate followed the donor, every time.

headline: So the clock
body: It's inside the plate itself. Not your hormones, not your age, not some central signal telling your bones when to quit.
punch: The plate carries its own history, and that history is what runs out.

headline: What actually runs out
body: Resting-zone chondrocytes have a finite replicative capacity. Every division spends a little of it. When the pool is depleted, columns thin out, growth decelerates, and the plate finally ossifies.
punch: It's a bank account, not a timer. Nothing refills it.

headline: Which is why growth slows
body: Deceleration comes first. Fusion follows it, sometimes long after.
punch: The closed plate on an X-ray is the receipt for capacity already spent — not the event that stopped you growing.

headline: Here's the part
body: Suppress growth temporarily and plates grow faster than expected afterward. Catch-up growth. If fusion ran on a clock, lost time would be lost forever.
punch: It isn't — because slowing division conserves the account instead of draining it.

headline: So the real target
body: It's preserving proliferative capacity. Those sound identical and aren't.
punch: Confusing them is why so much height advice optimises the wrong variable — chasing a date instead of the resource that sets it.

headline: And the honest part
body: Four competing theories for how fusion executes at the cellular level: apoptosis, autophagy, hypoxia, transdifferentiation. None confirmed in humans — one human study found no classical apoptosis at all.
punch: Anyone certain here hasn't read the papers.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
